option_description: Controls whether an automated configuration management tool actively enforces approved security baselines across all system instances at deployment time, not merely reporting deviations.
security_impact: The Rego policy grants the baseline_configuration_enforcement countermeasure only when this attribute is true AND compliance_scan_status is compliant. Without active enforcement mode, configuration management tools default to audit-only behavior, allowing non-compliant configurations to persist indefinitely. This exposes systems to misconfiguration-based attacks mapped to MITRE M1054 (Software Configuration) and M1028 (OS Configuration).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Ansible Tower/AWX job templates for enforce mode by querying the API for playbook enforcement settings
how_to_obtain.command: ansible-tower-cli job_template list --format json | jq '.results[] | {name: .name, job_type: .job_type}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: job_type should be 'run' with remediation playbooks active, not just check mode

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify AWS Config rules are in enforcement mode rather than audit-only mode
how_to_obtain.command: aws configservice describe-config-rules --query 'ConfigRules[*].{Name:ConfigRuleName,State:ConfigRuleState}' --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ConfigRuleState should be ACTIVE; cross-reference with remediation actions via aws configservice describe-remediation-configurations

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to Azure Policy in the Azure Portal and verify assignments are set to DeployIfNotExists or Deny effect rather than Audit
how_to_obtain.navigation: Azure Portal > Policy > Assignments > select assignment > review Effect parameter for each policy definition
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Effect should be 'DeployIfNotExists' or 'Deny', not 'Audit' or 'Disabled'

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Puppet or Chef configuration to confirm enforcement runmode is not set to noop (no-operation/audit-only)
how_to_obtain.command: puppet config print noop --section agent
how_to_obtain.expected_output: noop = false confirms enforcement is active; 'true' means audit-only mode

option_description: Records the outcome of the most recent automated compliance scan comparing live system configuration against the approved security baseline, indicating whether the environment is fully compliant, partially compliant, non-compliant, or has not been scanned.
security_impact: The Rego policy requires compliance_scan_status to equal compliant before the baseline_configuration_enforcement countermeasure is credited. A status of non_compliant, partially_compliant, or not_scanned causes the countermeasure to fail even if baseline_enforcement_enabled is true. This attribute serves as the evidence of actual enforcement effectiveness, not just tool presence.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query AWS Config aggregated compliance summary for all config rules across the account
how_to_obtain.command: aws configservice get-compliance-summary-by-config-rule --query 'ComplianceSummariesByConfigRule[*].{Rule:ConfigRuleName,Compliance:Compliance.ComplianceType}' --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All rules should return COMPLIANT; NON_COMPLIANT entries require remediation before setting this attribute to compliant

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run a CIS-CAT Pro scan against the host and capture the overall compliance percentage
how_to_obtain.command: sh CIS-CAT.sh -a -b benchmarks/CIS_Ubuntu_Linux_22.04_LTS_Benchmark_v1.0.0-xccdf.xml 2>&1 | grep -E 'Compliance Score|Pass|Fail'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 100% compliance maps to compliant; any failures map to non_compliant or partially_compliant depending on rule count

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the Azure Policy compliance dashboard for the policy initiative assigned to the resource group or subscription
how_to_obtain.navigation: Azure Portal > Policy > Compliance > select initiative > review Overall Compliance percentage and non-compliant resource count
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 100% compliant resources with 0 non-compliant resources maps to compliant status

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use OpenSCAP to scan a system against a defined XCCDF profile and extract pass/fail summary
how_to_obtain.command: oscap xccdf eval --profile xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_profile_cis --results scan-results.xml /usr/share/xml/scap/ssg/content/ssg-rhel9-ds.xml && oscap xccdf generate report scan-results.xml | grep -E 'pass|fail|Score'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Score of 100% with no failures corresponds to compliant; partial failures to partially_compliant; widespread failures to non_compliant

option_description: Indicates whether a continuous or scheduled automated monitoring mechanism is actively running to detect deviations from the approved configuration baseline after initial deployment, distinct from one-time scanning.
security_impact: The Rego policy references drift_detection_enabled across three rules: baseline_configuration_enforcement (as a supporting condition), configuration_drift_detection (as a required condition), and immutable_infrastructure_provisioning (as a supporting signal). Without drift detection enabled, configuration changes made post-deployment go undetected, allowing adversaries to maintain persistence through configuration manipulation aligned with MITRE M1047 (Audit) gaps.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify AWS Config continuous recording is enabled for all resource types in the account
how_to_obtain.command: aws configservice describe-configuration-recorders --query 'ConfigurationRecorders[*].{Name:name,AllSupported:recordingGroup.allSupported,RecordingEnabled:recordingGroup.allSupported}' --output json && aws configservice describe-configuration-recorder-status --query 'ConfigurationRecordersStatus[*].{Name:name,Recording:recording,LastStatus:lastStatus}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: recording: true and lastStatus: SUCCESS confirms continuous drift detection is active

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for active Ansible drift detection cron jobs or scheduled AWX job templates
how_to_obtain.command: crontab -l | grep -i ansible; systemctl list-timers | grep ansible; ansible-tower-cli schedule list --format json | jq '.results[] | {name: .name, enabled: .enabled, next_run: .next_run}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Scheduled jobs with enabled: true and a future next_run timestamp confirm drift detection is active

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Chef Infra client configuration to confirm scheduled convergence runs are active
how_to_obtain.command: systemctl is-enabled chef-client && systemctl status chef-client | grep -E 'Active|Next'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: enabled and active (running) status with a scheduled interval confirms drift detection via convergence

how_to_obtain.instruction: Confirm AWS Config is recording and that Config Rules have periodic evaluation triggers enabled
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > Config > Settings > verify Recording is ON; Config > Rules > select rule > verify Trigger type includes Periodic
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Recording status ON and trigger type showing Periodic or Configuration changes confirms drift detection is enabled

option_description: Captures the maturity state of the formal configuration baseline—whether no baseline exists, one has been defined but is not actively enforced by tooling, or a versioned baseline is both documented and referenced by the drift detection mechanism.
security_impact: The configuration_drift_detection Rego rule requires baseline_definition_status to equal defined_and_enforced. A value of none or defined_not_enforced means drift detection has no authoritative reference state to compare against, rendering monitoring meaningless. Without an enforced baseline, deviations cannot be reliably identified or remediated, undermining MITRE D3-OPM (Operational Process Monitoring) defenses.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether a version-controlled IaC state file or golden image manifest is committed to the repository and referenced by configuration tooling
how_to_obtain.command: git -C /path/to/iac-repo log --oneline -5 -- baseline/ security-baseline.yml hardening/; terraform show -json terraform.tfstate | jq '.values.root_module.resources | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Recent commits to baseline files and a non-zero resource count in state confirm a defined baseline exists in version control

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the AWS Config conformance pack or custom Config rule source to verify it references a defined baseline document
how_to_obtain.command: aws configservice describe-conformance-packs --query 'ConformancePackDetails[*].{Name:ConformancePackName,Status:ConformancePackState}' --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Status of CREATE_COMPLETE with referenced conformance pack confirms baseline is defined and enforced

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the infrastructure or security team to determine whether a CIS benchmark, STIG, or custom hardening guide has been formally adopted and linked to automation tooling
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response should identify a specific named document (e.g., CIS Ubuntu 22.04 Level 2), its version, and the tool enforcing it (e.g., Chef cookbook, Ansible role)

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that Chef cookbooks or Ansible roles reference a defined baseline profile and are not operating without a compliance target
how_to_obtain.command: inspec check /path/to/baseline-profile && inspec exec /path/to/baseline-profile --reporter json | jq '.profiles[].controls | length'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Non-zero control count and successful check output confirms a baseline profile is defined and executable

option_description: Determines whether the drift detection mechanism is configured to actively notify security or operations teams—via email, SIEM, ticketing system, or webhook—when a configuration deviation from the baseline is detected.
security_impact: The configuration_drift_detection Rego rule mandates alert_on_drift be true alongside drift detection and baseline definition. Without alerting, drift may be detected internally by tooling but never surfaced to responders, leaving the D3-OPM (Operational Process Monitoring) defense theoretically present but operationally ineffective. Silent drift allows adversaries to maintain unauthorized configuration changes indefinitely.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check AWS Config SNS notification channels to verify alerts are forwarded to a topic upon rule non-compliance
how_to_obtain.command: aws configservice describe-delivery-channels --query 'DeliveryChannels[*].{Name:name,SNSTopic:snsTopicARN}' --output table && aws sns list-subscriptions-by-topic --topic-arn <SNS_TOPIC_ARN> --query 'Subscriptions[*].{Protocol:Protocol,Endpoint:Endpoint}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A populated SNSTopic ARN and at least one active subscription (email, SQS, HTTPS/webhook) confirms alerting is configured

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify Azure Policy is connected to Azure Monitor alert rules or Event Grid subscriptions that trigger on compliance state changes
how_to_obtain.navigation: Azure Portal > Monitor > Alerts > Alert Rules > filter by signal type Policy > verify at least one active rule targeting non-compliant resources with an action group configured
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one enabled alert rule with a configured action group (email, Logic App, webhook) confirms alerting on drift

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Ansible AWX/Tower notification templates associated with job templates that perform drift detection
how_to_obtain.command: ansible-tower-cli notification_template list --format json | jq '.results[] | {name: .name, type: .notification_type, active: .active}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: At least one active notification template of type email, slack, or webhook linked to drift detection job templates confirms alerting

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Chef Infra or InSpec configuration for handler or reporter integrations that forward compliance failures to SIEM or ticketing
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rE 'reporter|handler|siem|splunk|webhook|pagerduty|jira' /etc/chef/client.rb /etc/inspec/ 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of configured reporters (e.g., json-rsa, splunk-reporter) or handlers confirms drift alerts are forwarded externally

option_description: Specifies the interval in hours between automated drift detection scans, where 0 indicates continuous or event-driven detection and values above 24 indicate potentially insufficient detection frequency for high-criticality environments.
security_impact: The configuration_drift_detection Rego rule enforces detection_frequency_hours <= 24 as a hard threshold. Detection intervals exceeding 24 hours create prolonged windows during which an adversary can exploit misconfigured systems without triggering the MITRE D3-OPM monitoring defense. Event-driven (0) or hourly scans dramatically reduce mean time to detect unauthorized configuration changes.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve the evaluation frequency for periodic AWS Config rules in hours
how_to_obtain.command: aws configservice describe-config-rules --query 'ConfigRules[?Source.Owner==`AWS` || Source.Owner==`CUSTOM_LAMBDA`].{Name:ConfigRuleName,Frequency:MaximumExecutionFrequency}' --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: MaximumExecutionFrequency values: One_Hour=1, Three_Hours=3, Six_Hours=6, Twelve_Hours=12, TwentyFour_Hours=24; continuous recording shows as null (effectively 0)

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the Chef client daemon run interval to determine how frequently drift detection convergence runs occur
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E '^interval|^splay' /etc/chef/client.rb; systemctl cat chef-client | grep -E 'OnCalendar|OnBootSec|OnUnitActiveSec'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: interval = 1800 means 0.5 hours; divide seconds by 3600 to get hours; OnUnitActiveSec=1h confirms 1-hour frequency

how_to_obtain.instruction: List scheduled Ansible playbook runs and calculate frequency in hours from cron expression or AWX schedule
how_to_obtain.command: crontab -l | grep -i ansible | awk '{print "Min:", $1, "Hr:", $2, "Day:", $3}'; ansible-tower-cli schedule list --format json | jq '.results[] | {name: .name, rrule: .rrule}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RRULE:FREQ=HOURLY;INTERVAL=1 maps to 1 hour; FREQ=DAILY maps to 24 hours; parse INTERVAL value to determine scan frequency

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect InSpec compliance scan scheduling configuration for interval settings
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rE 'interval|schedule|cron|frequency' /etc/inspec/ /etc/cinc-auditor/ 2>/dev/null; crontab -l | grep -i inspec
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Cron expression or interval value indicating scan frequency; convert to hours (e.g., */6 * = every 6 hours)

option_description: Describes whether infrastructure instances are deployed from versioned, read-only artifacts such as container images, VM snapshots, or AMIs and replaced entirely on change rather than modified in place, classifying the model as fully image-based, partially immutable, or fully mutable.
security_impact: The immutable_infrastructure_provisioning Rego rule requires immutable_deployment_model to equal image_based as the primary condition. Mutable or partial models allow in-place modifications that circumvent baseline enforcement, as changes bypass the IaC pipeline entirely. An image_based model supports MITRE D3-EI (Execution Isolation) and D3-PH (Platform Hardening) by ensuring every running instance is traceable to a known, validated artifact.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that EC2 instances are launched from hardened AMIs and that no instances allow SSH-based in-place modification by checking instance launch configurations
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-instances --query 'Reservations[*].Instances[*].{Id:InstanceId,AMI:ImageId,KeyName:KeyName,LaunchTime:LaunchTime}' --output table; aws ec2 describe-images --owners self --query 'Images[*].{Id:ImageId,Name:Name,Created:CreationDate,State:State}' --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All instances launched from organization-owned AMIs with no direct key-pair SSH access confirms image_based; key-pair access present indicates mutable or partial

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Kubernetes deployment specifications to confirm containers use immutable image tags (digest-pinned) rather than mutable tags like 'latest'
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get deployments,daemonsets,statefulsets --all-namespaces -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{range .spec.template.spec.containers[*]}{.image}{"\n"}{end}{end}' | grep -E ':latest|:[a-z]+-[a-z]+$|:[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No results (no mutable tags) confirms image_based model; presence of :latest or non-digest tags indicates mutable or partial

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Terraform or Packer configuration to confirm infrastructure is defined as immutable image builds with no post-deployment provisioners that modify running instances
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rE 'user_data|provisioner|remote-exec|in_place|mutable' /path/to/terraform/; cat /path/to/packer/*.json | jq '.provisioners[].type'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Absence of remote-exec provisioners and presence of AMI/image_id references confirms image_based; remote-exec or user_data scripts modifying running instances indicate mutable

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the DevOps team to determine the change management process: are configuration changes made by rebuilding and redeploying images, or by running scripts against live instances
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Process of rebuild-and-replace with no direct SSH/RDP access to running instances confirms image_based; documented runbook steps for in-place changes confirm mutable or partial

option_description: Controls whether runtime modifications to running instances—such as SSH/RDP access for configuration changes, package installations, or direct file edits—are technically permitted and not blocked by policy or tooling.
security_impact: The Rego policy for immutable_infrastructure_provisioning requires this attribute to be false. If in-place modification is permitted, the immutable infrastructure countermeasure cannot be satisfied, leaving systems vulnerable to unauthorized configuration changes, configuration drift, and untracked state mutations that bypass the intended deployment pipeline.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check AWS security groups and IAM policies for SSH/RDP access to EC2 instances to determine whether port 22 or 3389 is reachable and whether IAM allows SSM Session Manager interactive sessions.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters 'Name=ip-permission.from-port,Values=22' --query 'SecurityGroups[*].{ID:GroupId,Name:GroupName,Ingress:IpPermissions}' --output table && aws iam list-policies --scope Local --query 'Policies[*].PolicyName'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No security groups should return port 22/3389 open to 0.0.0.0/0 or broad CIDR ranges. IAM policies should deny ec2-instance-connect and ssm:StartSession actions on production instances.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the AWS Console, navigate to EC2 > Security Groups and filter for rules permitting inbound TCP 22 or 3389. Also check AWS Systems Manager > Session Manager > Preferences to see whether interactive sessions are enabled for production instance fleets.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > EC2 > Security Groups > Inbound Rules filter (Port: 22 or 3389); AWS Console > Systems Manager > Session Manager > Preferences
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Production security groups show no inbound rules permitting SSH/RDP. Session Manager logging is enforced and direct shell access is disabled via IAM conditions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Terraform or CloudFormation IaC templates defining security group rules and IAM policies to confirm no rules permit port 22 or 3389 ingress on production resources.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'from_port.*22\|to_port.*22\|from_port.*3389\|to_port.*3389' ./infrastructure/ --include='*.tf' --include='*.yaml' --include='*.json'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No matches for port 22 or 3389 in production security group definitions, or all matches include explicit deny conditions limiting access to emergency break-glass procedures only.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform or DevOps team to determine whether any operational runbooks or emergency procedures authorize SSH/RDP access to running production instances and whether this is documented as an exception.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No standing SSH/RDP access to production instances. Any emergency access is gated behind a break-glass process with mandatory MFA, time-limited credentials, and full session logging.

typical_values: false (immutable environments with no direct access)
true (legacy environments with config management agents that SSH in)

option_description: Controls whether cryptographic integrity checks—such as image signing (Cosign, Notary), digest pinning, or checksum verification—are enforced before build artifacts are deployed, ensuring only approved and unmodified images reach production.
security_impact: The Rego policy for immutable_infrastructure_provisioning requires this attribute to be true alongside in_place_modification_permitted being false. Without artifact integrity validation, malicious or corrupted images could be deployed even in otherwise immutable environments, undermining the entire immutable infrastructure countermeasure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether Cosign or Notary is configured in the CI/CD pipeline by inspecting pipeline configuration files and verifying that image signatures exist in the container registry for current production images.
how_to_obtain.command: cosign verify --certificate-identity-regexp='.*' --certificate-oidc-issuer-regexp='.*' <registry>/<image>:<tag> 2>&1 && kubectl get constrainttemplate requiredsignedimages -o yaml 2>/dev/null || echo 'No OPA constraint found'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Cosign verify returns a valid signature payload with the expected issuer and subject. OPA/Gatekeeper constraint template exists and is in enforcement mode for image signature validation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect CI/CD pipeline configuration files (GitHub Actions workflows, GitLab CI, Jenkins pipelines) for image signing steps and admission controller policies for signature enforcement.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'cosign\|notary\|image-sign\|COSIGN_EXPERIMENTAL\|digest\|sha256' .github/workflows/ .gitlab-ci.yml Jenkinsfile 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pipeline definitions contain explicit cosign sign or notation sign steps after image build, and a cosign verify or equivalent step before deployment promotion.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the container registry API to confirm that image manifests include signatures or that only digest-pinned references are used in deployment manifests.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ecr describe-images --repository-name <repo-name> --query 'imageDetails[*].{Tags:imageTags,Digest:imageDigest,Pushed:imagePushedAt}' --output table && aws ecr get-image --repository-name <repo-name> --image-id imageTag=latest --query 'image.imageManifest'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Images in the registry have associated signature objects (cosign attaches them as separate tags or OCI artifacts). Kubernetes manifests reference images by digest (sha256:...) rather than mutable tags.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the container registry console (ECR, GCR, ACR, or Docker Hub), check whether image signing is enabled and review deployment admission policies in the Kubernetes cluster's OPA/Gatekeeper or Kyverno policy engine.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > ECR > Repositories > Select Repo > Images (verify digest references); Kubernetes Dashboard or kubectl: kubectl get policies -n gatekeeper-system
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Registry shows signed images with attestation metadata. Admission controller policies exist in 'enforce' mode requiring valid signatures before pods are scheduled.

typical_values: false (common in organizations without supply chain security maturity)
true (organizations with DevSecOps pipelines using Cosign or Notary with OPA enforcement)

option_description: Controls whether a dedicated secrets management solution (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager) is integrated into the provisioning pipeline so that credentials are retrieved dynamically at runtime rather than baked into artifacts or configuration files.
security_impact: The Rego policy for secrets_and_credential_injection_control requires this to be true, combined with hardcoded_secrets_detected being false and an approved secret_injection_method. Without secrets manager integration, credentials are likely embedded in static configuration, environment files, or IaC templates, creating long-lived exposure risk and violating the credential hardening countermeasure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review IaC templates, deployment scripts, and application configuration files for references to secrets manager APIs, Vault agent injector annotations, or external secrets operator configurations.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'secretsmanager\|vault\.hashicorp\|keyvault\|SecretId\|vault-agent\|external-secrets\|SecretProviderClass' ./infrastructure/ ./k8s/ ./helm/ --include='*.yaml' --include='*.tf' --include='*.json' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Kubernetes pods have vault-agent-injector annotations or ExternalSecret/SecretProviderClass objects. Terraform references data.aws_secretsmanager_secret or data.vault_generic_secret data sources.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check AWS Secrets Manager for secrets associated with the application and verify IAM roles attached to compute resources have GetSecretValue permissions, indicating the application is designed to retrieve secrets at runtime.
how_to_obtain.command: aws secretsmanager list-secrets --query 'SecretList[*].{Name:Name,ARN:ARN,LastRotated:LastRotatedDate}' --output table && aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn <instance-role-arn> --action-names secretsmanager:GetSecretValue --resource-arns '*' --query 'EvaluationResults[*].{Action:EvalActionName,Decision:EvalDecision}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Secrets exist in Secrets Manager with recent rotation dates. The instance/pod IAM role has Allow decisions for secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on specific secret ARNs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In AWS Console, navigate to Secrets Manager to verify secrets are defined for the application. Then check the application's ECS task definition or EC2 instance profile to confirm it references secrets via the secrets or environment valueFrom syntax.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > Secrets Manager > Secrets list; AWS Console > ECS > Task Definitions > Container Definitions > Environment > Secrets section
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ECS task definition shows secrets sourced from Secrets Manager ARNs using the valueFrom syntax. No plaintext values appear in environment variable definitions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the DevOps or platform engineering team to confirm whether a secrets management platform is part of the standard provisioning pipeline and whether developers are required to use it for all credential types.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Team can describe the secrets manager integration pattern, reference documentation or runbooks for adding new secrets, and confirm that pipeline gates exist to prevent plaintext credentials from reaching deployment artifacts.

typical_values: false (small teams or legacy systems using .env files or SSM Parameter Store without enforced pipeline integration)
true (mature DevSecOps environments with Vault or cloud-native secrets manager wired into CI/CD)

option_description: Indicates whether plaintext secrets, passwords, API keys, tokens, or private key material have been detected embedded directly in configuration files, IaC templates, scripts, or source code repositories.
security_impact: The Rego policy for secrets_and_credential_injection_control requires this to be false. Any hardcoded secret represents a critical exposure because it persists in version history, is accessible to anyone with repository access, and cannot be rotated without a code change—directly undermining the credential hardening and credential rotation countermeasures.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run truffleHog against the repository to detect high-entropy strings and known secret patterns across the full git history, including all branches and commits.
how_to_obtain.command: trufflehog git file://. --only-verified --json 2>/dev/null | jq '{source: .SourceMetadata.Data.Git.file, line: .SourceMetadata.Data.Git.line, detector: .DetectorName, verified: .Verified}' || trufflehog filesystem . --json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Zero verified findings returned. Unverified findings may indicate false positives but should be reviewed. Any output indicates hardcoded_secrets_detected should be set to true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run detect-secrets to scan the current working tree for secret patterns and compare against an existing baseline to identify new additions.
how_to_obtain.command: detect-secrets scan --all-files --list-all-plugins 2>/dev/null && detect-secrets scan . | detect-secrets audit - || pip install detect-secrets && detect-secrets scan --baseline .secrets.baseline .
how_to_obtain.expected_output: detect-secrets returns no new unaudited findings beyond the approved baseline. A clean baseline file exists and is maintained in the repository.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use git-secrets to check the repository for common credential patterns such as AWS access keys, generic passwords, and private keys.
how_to_obtain.command: git secrets --scan-history 2>/dev/null || (git secrets --register-aws && git secrets --scan-history) && grep -rn 'password\s*=\s*['"]\|api_key\s*=\s*['"]\|secret\s*=\s*['"]\|BEGIN.*PRIVATE KEY' . --include='*.tf' --include='*.yaml' --include='*.env' --include='*.json' --include='*.sh' | grep -v '.git/'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: git secrets reports no violations across commit history. grep returns no matches, or all matches reference variable names rather than literal values (e.g., secret = var.db_password rather than secret = 'P@ssword123').

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use GitHub Advanced Security or GitLab Secret Detection API to retrieve secret scanning alerts for the repository if the platform supports it.
how_to_obtain.command: gh api /repos/{owner}/{repo}/secret-scanning/alerts --paginate --jq '.[] | select(.state=="open") | {secret_type: .secret_type, location: .locations_url, created: .created_at}' 2>/dev/null || curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer $GITLAB_TOKEN' 'https://gitlab.com/api/v4/projects/<id>/vulnerability_findings?scanner=secret_detection&state=opened'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Zero open secret scanning alerts in the repository. If alerts exist, each must be triaged—true positives confirm hardcoded_secrets_detected should be true.

typical_values: false (expected baseline for compliant repositories with enforced pre-commit hooks and pipeline scanning)
true (legacy repositories, rushed development cycles, or environments without mandatory secret scanning gates)

option_description: Specifies the mechanism by which secrets and credentials are delivered to the running environment at provisioning time, ranging from dynamic vault generation through encrypted injection down to plaintext environment variables or no injection mechanism.
security_impact: The Rego policy for secrets_and_credential_injection_control requires this value to be one of vault_dynamic, secrets_manager_api, or encrypted_env_injection. Values of plaintext_env or none prevent the countermeasure from being satisfied. vault_dynamic provides the strongest posture through short-lived dynamic credentials, while secrets_manager_api and encrypted_env_injection are acceptable. Plaintext injection exposes credentials in process environment tables visible to any local process.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Kubernetes deployment manifests, ECS task definitions, or Docker Compose files to identify how secrets reach containers—via volume mounts from CSI drivers, environment valueFrom secretsmanager, or literal env values.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get deployment <deployment-name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[*].env}' | python3 -m json.tool && kubectl get deployment <deployment-name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.volumes}' | python3 -m json.tool
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Container env blocks show valueFrom.secretKeyRef references backed by ExternalSecrets or SecretProviderClass (secrets_manager_api or vault_dynamic). No literal value fields containing credential material.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for Vault Agent Injector annotations on pods or Vault sidecar containers that indicate dynamic secret generation and injection.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{.metadata.annotations}{"\n"}{end}' | grep -A5 'vault.hashicorp.com' && kubectl get pods -n <namespace> -o json | jq '.items[].spec.initContainers[]? | select(.name | contains("vault")) | {name: .name, image: .image}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pods have vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: 'true' annotations or vault-agent init containers present, confirming vault_dynamic injection. Template annotations reference specific secret paths in Vault.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the ECS task definition API or Lambda function configuration to determine whether secrets are sourced from Secrets Manager (secrets_manager_api) or passed as plaintext environment variables.
how_to_obtain.command: aws ecs describe-task-definition --task-definition <task-def-name> --query 'taskDefinition.containerDefinitions[*].{Name:name,Env:environment,Secrets:secrets}' --output json | python3 -m json.tool && aws lambda get-function-configuration --function-name <function-name> --query '{Env:Environment.Variables,Layers:Layers}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ECS task definition shows a populated secrets array with valueFrom pointing to Secrets Manager ARNs (confirming secrets_manager_api). The environment array should not contain credential key names with literal values.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the application onboarding documentation and developer guidelines to understand the mandated secret injection pattern and whether engineers are trained to use a specific method.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation explicitly mandates vault_dynamic or secrets_manager_api injection. Runbooks for adding new application secrets describe the approved process and reject plaintext environment variable patterns.

typical_values: vault_dynamic (organizations using HashiCorp Vault with agent injection or dynamic secrets)
secrets_manager_api (AWS/Azure/GCP native environments using cloud secrets managers)
encrypted_env_injection (environments using SOPS or sealed secrets)
plaintext_env (legacy environments or development workflows with unresolved debt)
none (environments with no formal secrets management)

option_description: Controls whether the configuration management system is set to automatically re-converge drifted systems back to their intended baseline state without requiring manual operator intervention.
security_impact: The Rego policy for automated_remediation_response requires this to be true along with remediation_mode being enforced. Without auto-remediation, detected configuration drift remains in place until an operator acts, creating a window where systems operate in a non-compliant and potentially vulnerable state. The policy reduces MTTR to zero for known drift patterns.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check AWS Config Rules or AWS Systems Manager State Manager to determine whether remediation actions are configured and set to automatic execution rather than requiring manual approval.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > Config > Rules > Select Rule > Remediation actions (check 'Auto remediation' checkbox status); AWS Console > Systems Manager > State Manager > Associations > Compliance Severity and Schedule
how_to_obtain.expected_output: AWS Config rules show 'Auto remediation' enabled with a linked SSM Automation document. State Manager associations show a recurring schedule with automatic execution (not manual approval required).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query AWS Config for all rules and check whether automatic remediation configurations are attached and enabled.
how_to_obtain.command: aws configservice describe-remediation-configurations --config-rule-names $(aws configservice describe-config-rules --query 'ConfigRules[*].ConfigRuleName' --output text) --query 'RemediationConfigurations[*].{Rule:ConfigRuleName,Auto:Automatic,TargetId:TargetId}' --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All remediation configurations show Automatic: true. Rules without remediation configurations attached represent gaps where auto-remediation is not enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Puppet, Chef, or Ansible configuration management settings to confirm enforcement mode (agent runs, continuous enforcement intervals) is active rather than noop/check mode.
how_to_obtain.command: puppet config print noop --section agent 2>/dev/null && puppet agent --configprint runinterval 2>/dev/null || ansible-lint --list-tags site.yml 2>/dev/null && grep -r 'noop\|check_mode\|--check' /etc/puppet/ /etc/chef/ ./ansible.cfg 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Puppet noop returns 'false'. Chef client is not in why-run mode. Ansible playbooks do not have check_mode: true set globally. This confirms auto-remediation enforcement is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Azure Policy or GCP Organization Policy APIs to confirm whether policy assignments are in 'DeployIfNotExists' or 'Modify' effect mode (auto-remediation) rather than 'Audit' or 'Deny' only.
how_to_obtain.command: az policy assignment list --query '[*].{Name:name,EnforcementMode:enforcementMode,PolicyDef:policyDefinitionId}' --output table 2>/dev/null || gcloud asset search-all-resources --asset-types='cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com/Project' --query 'policy' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Azure Policy assignments show enforcementMode: Default (not DoNotEnforce). Policy definitions use DeployIfNotExists or Modify effects rather than AuditIfNotExists only.

typical_values: false (audit-only configurations common in organizations prioritizing visibility over enforcement)
true (mature environments with tested remediation playbooks and change management processes that support automated correction)

option_description: Specifies the operational mode of the configuration enforcement system—whether it only audits and reports violations, actively alerts, or enforces compliance and automatically remediates drift without operator involvement.
security_impact: The Rego policy for automated_remediation_response requires this to be enforced. An audit or disabled mode means the policy engine detects drift but takes no corrective action, leaving systems in non-compliant states indefinitely. Only enforced mode satisfies the countermeasure and ensures mean time to remediation is bounded by the max_remediation_interval_minutes value.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query AWS Config rule details and remediation configurations to determine whether rules are in audit-only mode or have active enforcement with automatic remediation enabled.
how_to_obtain.command: aws configservice describe-config-rules --query 'ConfigRules[*].{Name:ConfigRuleName,Source:Source.Owner,ComplianceType:MaximumExecutionFrequency}' --output table && aws configservice describe-remediation-configurations --config-rule-names $(aws configservice describe-config-rules --query 'ConfigRules[*].ConfigRuleName' --output text 2>/dev/null) --query 'RemediationConfigurations[*].{Rule:ConfigRuleName,Automatic:Automatic}' --output table 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Config rules with Automatic: true in remediation configurations confirm enforced mode. Rules with no remediation configuration or Automatic: false are in audit mode only.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Puppet agent configuration for noop mode, Chef client for why-run mode, or Ansible Tower/AWX job templates for check mode to determine the effective enforcement posture.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'noop|why_run|check_mode|enforce' /etc/puppet/puppet.conf /etc/chef/client.rb /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg 2>/dev/null && systemctl show puppet --property=ExecStart 2>/dev/null | grep -o 'noop' || echo 'noop flag not detected in puppet service'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No noop, why_run, or check_mode flags are active. Puppet conf shows noop = false. Chef client.rb does not include why_run true. This confirms enforced mode.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In HashiCorp Terraform Cloud or Sentinel policy sets, review whether policy checks are set to hard-mandatory (enforced) or advisory (audit). In OPA/Gatekeeper, check whether ConstraintTemplates are in enforce or dryrun mode.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Terraform Cloud > Organization Settings > Policy Sets > Enforcement Level; kubectl get constrainttemplate -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}: {.spec.enforcementAction}{"\n"}{end}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Terraform Cloud policies show hard-mandatory enforcement level. Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplates show enforcementAction: deny rather than dryrun or warn.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Azure Policy assignments for enforcement mode settings to determine whether policies are actively enforcing or only auditing.
how_to_obtain.command: az policy assignment list --query '[*].{Name:displayName,Mode:enforcementMode,Effect:parameters.effect.value}' --output table 2>/dev/null && az policy state list --query '[?complianceState==`NonCompliant`] | length(@)' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy assignments with enforcementMode: Default and effects of DeployIfNotExists or Modify confirm enforced mode. DoNotEnforce assignments confirm audit mode only.

typical_values: audit (default for most new deployments; organizations cautious about automated changes in production)
enforced (mature environments with validated remediation playbooks; required for automated_remediation_response countermeasure)
disabled (environments where configuration management tooling is installed but inactive)

option_description: Specifies the maximum elapsed time in minutes between the detection of configuration drift and the automated re-convergence being triggered. Lower values indicate more responsive remediation, with 0 indicating near-real-time enforcement.
security_impact: The Rego policy for automated_remediation_response requires this value to be 60 or less (one hour) when auto-remediation is enabled and mode is enforced. A high interval (up to the maximum of 10080 minutes, or one week) means drifted systems remain non-compliant for extended periods, providing adversaries with a prolonged window to exploit misconfigured states. Values above 60 minutes fail the countermeasure condition.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the Puppet agent run interval or Chef client run interval configured on managed nodes to determine how frequently the agent enforces configuration convergence.
how_to_obtain.command: puppet config print runinterval --section agent 2>/dev/null && echo 'Puppet interval (seconds)' || chef-client --version 2>/dev/null && grep -E 'interval|splay' /etc/chef/client.rb 2>/dev/null && systemctl show puppet --property=ExecStart 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Puppet runinterval shows a value in seconds (divide by 60 for minutes); 1800 = 30 minutes is a common secure value. Chef interval from client.rb should be 1800 or less for compliant posture.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query AWS Config rule evaluation frequency and AWS Systems Manager State Manager association schedule to determine the maximum time between compliance checks and remediation execution.
how_to_obtain.command: aws configservice describe-config-rules --query 'ConfigRules[*].{Name:ConfigRuleName,Frequency:MaximumExecutionFrequency}' --output table && aws ssm list-associations --query 'Associations[*].{Name:Name,Schedule:ScheduleExpression,LastExec:LastExecutionDate}' --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Config rules show MaximumExecutionFrequency of TwentyFour_Hours or less (1440 minutes). State Manager associations show cron or rate schedules of rate(30 minutes) or similar. Values must total 60 minutes or less for policy compliance.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Ansible Tower/AWX job template schedules or CI/CD pipeline cron triggers that invoke configuration enforcement playbooks to determine the polling interval.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'schedule\|cron\|interval\|every' ./ansible-tower-config/ ./awx-manifests/ 2>/dev/null && crontab -l 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'ansible|puppet|chef|remediat'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Schedule definitions show cron expressions with intervals of 30-60 minutes (e.g., */30 * * * * or */60 * * * *). Intervals greater than 60 minutes indicate the max_remediation_interval_minutes threshold will exceed the policy requirement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the AWS Config console, review the evaluation frequency for each Config rule. In Puppet Enterprise console, review the agent run interval under Node Configuration. In Ansible Tower/AWX, review the schedule of enforcement job templates.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Console > Config > Rules > Select Rule > Trigger type and frequency; Puppet Enterprise Console > Nodes > Configuration > Agent Run Interval; Ansible Tower > Templates > Select Template > Schedules tab
how_to_obtain.expected_output: AWS Config rules show evaluation frequency of One_Hour or less. Puppet Enterprise shows agent run interval of 30 minutes. Ansible Tower schedules show execution every 30-60 minutes. Any value above 60 minutes requires remediation.

typical_values: 30 (Puppet/Chef default agent interval in minutes; strong posture)
60 (common AWS Config rule evaluation frequency; meets policy threshold)
1440 (AWS Config 24-hour evaluation; fails the <=60 minute policy requirement)
null/not configured (no scheduled remediation; auto-remediation likely not active)

option_description: Tracks whether configuration parameters across development, staging, and production environments are verified to be consistent and in parity with each other, indicating in_sync, drifted, or unverified states.
security_impact: The Rego policy for environment_parity_assurance activates when this attribute equals 'in_sync' combined with security_controls_reproduced_in_production being true. A 'drifted' or 'unverified' status means production may lack security controls validated in lower environments, creating exploitable gaps that bypass pre-production testing.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run a Terraform plan diff against each environment's state file to detect configuration divergence between staging and production.
how_to_obtain.command: terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars -state=prod.tfstate -detailed-exitcode 2>&1 | grep -E '(will be|must be|has changed)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Exit code 0 indicates no drift (in_sync); exit code 2 with changes listed indicates drifted state.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use AWS Config to query environment configuration compliance across accounts, comparing rule evaluations between staging and production.
how_to_obtain.command: aws configservice describe-compliance-by-config-rule --compliance-types NON_COMPLIANT --query 'ComplianceByConfigRules[*].{Rule:ConfigRuleName,Compliance:Compliance.ComplianceType}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An empty NON_COMPLIANT list across both environments indicates in_sync; discrepancies between environments indicate drifted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to Terraform Cloud or Atlantis workspace run history and compare the last successful apply timestamps and plan outputs between staging and production workspaces.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Terraform Cloud → Organization → Workspaces → [staging-workspace] vs [production-workspace] → Runs → Latest Apply → Compare resource change summaries
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Both workspaces show 'No changes. Infrastructure is up-to-date.' on their most recent plans, confirming in_sync status.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query AWS Config aggregator API to retrieve configuration snapshots across multiple accounts/regions and compare resource configurations programmatically.
how_to_obtain.command: aws configservice batch-get-aggregate-resource-config --configuration-aggregator-name myAggregator --resource-identifiers '[{"SourceAccountId":"111111111111","SourceRegion":"us-east-1","ResourceId":"sg-prod","ResourceType":"AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup"}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration JSON objects matching between staging and production resource identifiers confirm in_sync status.

option_description: Boolean indicator confirming whether all security controls validated in lower environments (development and staging) — such as WAF rules, network security groups, secrets management, and logging agents — are present and active in the production environment.
security_impact: The Rego policy for environment_parity_assurance requires this attribute to be true regardless of which rule branch fires. If false, security controls tested in staging may be absent in production, meaning attack vectors blocked in lower environments remain open in production where real data and users are exposed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Compare security group rules between staging and production VPCs using AWS CLI to verify network security controls are reproduced.
how_to_obtain.command: diff <(aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=tag:Environment,Values=staging --query 'SecurityGroups[*].IpPermissions' --output json | jq 'sort') <(aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=tag:Environment,Values=production --query 'SecurityGroups[*].IpPermissions' --output json | jq 'sort')
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Empty diff output indicates identical security group rules across environments, supporting a true value.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inventory WAF rule groups attached to staging vs production application load balancers and compare rule counts and rule IDs.
how_to_obtain.command: for env in staging production; do echo "=== $env ==="; aws wafv2 list-web-acls --scope REGIONAL --query 'WebACLs[*].{Name:Name,ARN:ARN}' --output table; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Matching WAF ACL names and rule group ARNs across environments confirms controls are reproduced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In AWS Security Hub, compare the security findings count and enabled security standards between staging and production accounts to verify consistent control coverage.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Security Hub → Summary → Filter by account → Compare 'Passed controls' percentage between staging account and production account under Security Standards
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Equal or higher passed control percentage in production vs staging with no missing controls indicates true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the deployment runbook or environment provisioning checklist to confirm a formal security control parity verification step is documented and signed off for each production release.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A completed checklist with sign-off confirming each security control from the staging inventory was verified present in production.

option_description: Describes whether environment provisioning is enforced through infrastructure-as-code tooling with automated drift detection, IaC without drift detection, manual processes, or not enforced at all, characterizing the rigor of configuration management.
security_impact: The Rego policy for environment_parity_assurance has a dedicated rule branch that fires when this attribute equals 'automated_iac_with_drift_detection' combined with security_controls_reproduced_in_production being true. Without automated IaC enforcement, manual changes can introduce security misconfigurations that go undetected, and environments diverge silently from their secure baselines.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect CI/CD pipeline configuration files to determine if IaC tooling is invoked and whether drift detection flags are enabled.
how_to_obtain.command: find . -name '*.yml' -o -name 'Jenkinsfile' -o -name '.gitlab-ci.yml' | xargs grep -l -E '(terraform|ansible|pulumi|cloudformation)' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pipeline files containing terraform plan/apply, ansible-playbook, or pulumi up steps with drift-check stages indicate automated_iac_with_drift_detection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check if Terraform Cloud or Atlantis is configured with drift detection schedules by querying workspace settings.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TFE_TOKEN' https://app.terraform.io/api/v2/organizations/$ORG/workspaces?search=production | jq '.data[].attributes | {name: .name, "auto-apply": ."auto-apply", "drift-detection": ."drift-detection"}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'drift-detection: true' in workspace attributes confirms automated_iac_with_drift_detection; absent or false indicates iac_without_drift_detection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review AWS Config rule compliance dashboard to determine if config rules are actively evaluating resources, indicating automated enforcement is in place.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS Config → Rules → View all rules → Check 'Last successful evaluation' timestamps and 'Compliance' column for active automated evaluation
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules with recent evaluation timestamps and active compliance states confirm automated IaC enforcement is operating.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform or DevOps engineering team to determine whether production changes must be submitted via pull request to an IaC repository and whether manual console changes are blocked via SCPs or IAM policies.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Confirmation that all production changes flow through a reviewed IaC pipeline with no standing console write access indicates automated_iac_with_drift_detection or at minimum iac_without_drift_detection.

option_description: Boolean flag indicating whether audit logging for configuration changes is currently enabled and actively recording on the system or platform, capturing all modifications to infrastructure and application configuration.
security_impact: The Rego policy for configuration_change_audit_logging requires audit_logging_enabled to be true as its first condition in all rule branches. Without audit logging enabled, no forensic trail exists for configuration changes, making it impossible to detect unauthorized modifications, reconstruct incident timelines, or satisfy compliance requirements for change accountability.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify AWS CloudTrail is enabled and logging management events including configuration changes across all regions.
how_to_obtain.command: aws cloudtrail describe-trails --query 'trailList[*].{Name:Name,MultiRegion:IsMultiRegionTrail,LoggingEnabled:LogFileValidationEnabled}' --output table && aws cloudtrail get-trail-status --name $(aws cloudtrail describe-trails --query 'trailList[0].TrailARN' --output text) --query '{IsLogging:IsLogging,LatestDeliveryTime:LatestDeliveryTime}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'IsLogging: true' with a recent LatestDeliveryTime confirms audit logging is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check if AWS Config recorder is enabled and actively recording resource configuration changes.
how_to_obtain.command: aws configservice describe-configuration-recorder-status --query 'ConfigurationRecordersStatus[*].{Name:name,Recording:recording,LastStatus:lastStatus}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'recording: true' and 'lastStatus: SUCCESS' confirms configuration change audit logging is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Ansible Tower or AWX configuration to verify audit logging settings are enabled in the application settings file.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E '(AUDIT_LOG|LOG_AGGREGATOR_ENABLED|ALLOW_OAUTH2_FOR_EXTERNAL_USERS)' /etc/tower/settings.py /etc/tower/conf.d/*.py 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: LOG_AGGREGATOR_ENABLED = True and AUDIT_LOG settings present and active confirms audit logging enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Terraform Cloud, verify audit logging is enabled at the organization level by checking the organization settings audit logs section.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Terraform Cloud → Organization Settings → Security → Audit Logging → Verify 'Audit logging' toggle is enabled and shows recent log entries
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Audit logging toggle in enabled state with recent timestamps visible in the audit log feed.

option_description: An array of data fields captured per configuration change event, specifying which metadata is recorded for each change, such as initiator identity, timestamp, previous state, and new state values.
security_impact: The Rego policy for configuration_change_audit_logging requires all four specific fields — 'initiator', 'timestamp', 'previous_state', and 'new_state' — to be present in this array before any rule branch can fire. Missing any of these fields means audit logs cannot support complete forensic reconstruction of who changed what, when, and from what prior state, critically weakening incident investigation capabilities.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve a sample configuration change event from AWS CloudTrail and inspect its structure to confirm all required fields are present.
how_to_obtain.command: aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=PutConfigRule --max-results 1 --query 'Events[0].CloudTrailEvent' --output text | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E '(userIdentity|eventTime|requestParameters|responseElements)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output containing userIdentity (initiator), eventTime (timestamp), requestParameters (new_state), and responseElements confirming all required fields are logged.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query a SIEM or log aggregator for a recent configuration change event and extract field names to verify completeness against the required field set.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -X POST '$ELASTICSEARCH_URL/config-audit-*/_search' -d '{"query":{"match":{"event.category":"configuration"}},"size":1}' | jq '.hits.hits[0]._source | keys'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Array of field names that must include 'initiator' (or mapped equivalent), 'timestamp', 'previous_state', and 'new_state' to satisfy the Rego policy conditions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the logging configuration for your configuration management tool (e.g., Chef Automate, Ansible Tower) to identify which event fields are included in audit log output schemas.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -A 20 'audit' /etc/chef-automate/config.toml 2>/dev/null || cat /etc/tower/conf.d/logging.py | grep -A 10 'LOGGING'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration blocks listing logged fields that include user/initiator, time/timestamp, before/previous_state, and after/new_state field mappings.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the AWS Config API to retrieve a configuration item history and confirm the captured fields include all required change metadata.
how_to_obtain.command: aws configservice get-resource-config-history --resource-type AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup --resource-id sg-0123456789abcdef0 --limit 2 --query 'configurationItems[*].{time:configurationItemCaptureTime,actor:relatedEvents,config:configuration}' --output json
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Response objects containing captureTime, relatedEvents (initiator trace), configuration (new_state), and supplementaryConfiguration providing before/after state comparison data.

option_description: Specifies the mechanism in place to prevent modification or deletion of audit logs after they are written, with options including immutable storage, cryptographic signing, centralized SIEM forwarding, or no protection.
security_impact: The Rego policy for configuration_change_audit_logging requires log_tamper_protection to be one of 'immutable_storage', 'cryptographic_signing', or 'centralized_siem' — 'none' fails all rule branches. Without tamper protection, an attacker who gains access can modify or delete audit logs to cover their tracks, eliminating the forensic value of the entire configuration change audit logging control.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check if S3 Object Lock is enabled on the CloudTrail log bucket to confirm immutable storage is configured.
how_to_obtain.command: BUCKET=$(aws cloudtrail describe-trails --query 'trailList[0].S3BucketName' --output text) && aws s3api get-object-lock-configuration --bucket $BUCKET --query 'ObjectLockConfiguration.{Status:ObjectLockEnabled,Mode:Rule.DefaultRetention.Mode}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: '{Status: Enabled, Mode: GOVERNANCE}' or '{Status: Enabled, Mode: COMPLIANCE}' confirms immutable_storage is active.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify CloudTrail log file validation (cryptographic signing via hash chaining) is enabled on active trails.
how_to_obtain.command: aws cloudtrail describe-trails --query 'trailList[*].{TrailName:Name,LogFileValidation:LogFileValidationEnabled,MultiRegion:IsMultiRegionTrail}' --output table
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'LogFileValidation: True' confirms cryptographic_signing tamper protection is in place for CloudTrail logs.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the SIEM forwarding configuration (e.g., Splunk forwarder, Elastic agent, Sentinel connector) to confirm audit logs are shipped to a centralized, access-controlled SIEM in real time.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /opt/splunkforwarder/etc/system/local/inputs.conf | grep -A 5 'monitor:///var/log/audit' && cat /etc/filebeat/filebeat.yml | grep -A 10 'output.elasticsearch'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active monitor or input stanzas pointing audit log paths to a remote SIEM output confirms centralized_siem tamper protection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the AWS S3 console, verify the CloudTrail log bucket has Object Lock and MFA Delete enabled to confirm immutable storage protection.
how_to_obtain.navigation: AWS S3 Console → Buckets → [cloudtrail-logs-bucket] → Properties → Object Lock: verify 'Enabled' → Bucket versioning: verify 'MFA delete: Enabled'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Object Lock showing 'Enabled' status with a retention policy configured confirms immutable_storage tamper protection.

option_description: Boolean flag indicating whether pre-deployment policy-as-code validation checks are actively enabled in the CI/CD or deployment pipeline, using tools such as OPA, Conftest, Checkov, or Sentinel to evaluate configurations before they are applied.
security_impact: The Rego policy for policy_as_code_validation requires policy_validation_enabled to be true as its first condition. If false, non-compliant configurations — such as overly permissive security groups, disabled encryption, or absent logging — can be deployed to production without any automated gate, bypassing the organization's security policy entirely.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect CI/CD pipeline definition files for policy validation tool invocations (Checkov, Conftest, OPA, Sentinel) to confirm they are present and not commented out.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn -E '(checkov|conftest|opa eval|sentinel apply|tfsec|terrascan)' .github/workflows/ .gitlab-ci.yml Jenkinsfile 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Active (non-commented) lines invoking policy validation tools in pipeline stage definitions confirm policy_validation_enabled is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for Checkov configuration files in the repository root indicating it is configured and integrated into the project.
how_to_obtain.command: find . -name '.checkov.yaml' -o -name '.checkov.yml' -o -name 'checkov.yaml' 2>/dev/null | xargs cat 2>/dev/null; ls -la .conftest.toml .opa/ policy/ policies/ 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of policy tool configuration files with defined check suites or policy directories confirms policy validation is configured and enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In GitHub Actions or GitLab CI, review the pipeline run history for a recent infrastructure change and verify a policy validation job or step completed before the deploy stage.
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitHub → Repository → Actions → Latest workflow run for IaC change → Expand pipeline DAG → Verify 'policy-check' or 'security-scan' job completed before 'deploy' job
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A completed policy validation job node in the pipeline DAG with a passed or failed status (not skipped) confirms policy_validation_enabled is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the GitHub Actions API to retrieve recent workflow runs and check if a policy validation job is present and executing in the pipeline.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN' 'https://api.github.com/repos/$ORG/$REPO/actions/runs?per_page=5' | jq '.workflow_runs[0].id' | xargs -I{} curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN' 'https://api.github.com/repos/$ORG/$REPO/actions/runs/{}/jobs' | jq '.jobs[].name' | grep -i -E '(policy|checkov|conftest|security|opa)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Job names matching policy validation tool names in the workflow run's job list confirm policy_validation_enabled is true.

option_description: Specifies whether policy validation failures block deployment (enforced), only produce warnings (advisory), or are completely disabled, determining whether the policy-as-code gate has real blocking power over the deployment pipeline.
security_impact: The Rego policy for policy_as_code_validation requires this attribute to equal 'enforced'. An 'advisory' mode means policy failures generate warnings that engineers can ignore and deploy anyway, providing no actual prevention of misconfigured infrastructure. Only 'enforced' mode guarantees that policy-violating configurations cannot reach production regardless of human decisions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect CI/CD pipeline configuration to determine if policy tool failures are configured to exit with non-zero codes that block pipeline progression.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -A 5 -B 5 -E '(checkov|conftest|sentinel|opa)' .github/workflows/*.yml 2>/dev/null | grep -E '(continue-on-error|soft-fail|--soft-fail|exit-code|failure-mode|allow-failure)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Absence of 'continue-on-error: true' or '--soft-fail' flags on policy check steps indicates enforced mode; presence of these flags indicates advisory mode.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Checkov or Conftest invocation flags in pipeline scripts to determine if soft-fail mode is enabled, which would indicate advisory rather than enforced mode.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'checkov' ./ --include='*.yml' --include='*.yaml' --include='Jenkinsfile' 2>/dev/null | grep -v '^Binary' | grep -E '(soft.fail|exit.code|--check|--skip)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Commands without '--soft-fail' flag and with default exit-code behavior confirm enforced mode; '--soft-fail' presence confirms advisory mode.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Terraform Cloud or Sentinel policy set configuration, verify the policy enforcement level is set to 'hard-mandatory' rather than 'soft-mandatory' or 'advisory'.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Terraform Cloud → Organization Settings → Policy Sets → [policy-set-name] → Policies → Review each policy's 'Enforcement level' column for 'hard-mandatory' vs 'soft-mandatory' vs 'advisory'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'hard-mandatory' enforcement level on all production-scoped policies confirms enforced mode; 'soft-mandatory' or 'advisory' indicates advisory mode.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Terraform Cloud API to retrieve policy set enforcement levels configured for the production workspace.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TFE_TOKEN' -H 'Content-Type: application/vnd.api+json' 'https://app.terraform.io/api/v2/organizations/$ORG/policy-sets' | jq '.data[].attributes | {name: .name, global: .global, enforcement: ."enforcement-level"}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy set objects with 'enforcement-level: hard-mandatory' scoped to production workspaces confirm enforced mode.

option_description: Controls the number of active security policy rules loaded and evaluated by the policy engine (OPA, Conftest, Sentinel) during pre-deployment validation runs. A zero value means no rules are being evaluated.
security_impact: The Rego policy condition `input.policy_rule_count > 0` must be satisfied for the policy_as_code_validation countermeasure to activate. If this value is 0, all pre-deployment configuration validation is effectively disabled, allowing non-compliant infrastructure definitions to be applied without any policy gate.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query an OPA server to count active policies loaded in the bundle
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s http://localhost:8181/v1/policies | jq '[.result[] | select(.ast.rules != null)] | map(.ast.rules | length) | add // 0'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: An integer representing the total number of active rules across all loaded OPA policies, e.g. 147

how_to_obtain.instruction: Count active Conftest policy files and rules in the policy directory
how_to_obtain.command: find ./policy -name '*.rego' -exec grep -c '^[[:space:]]*[a-z_].*\[' {} + 2>/dev/null | awk -F: '{sum += $2} END {print sum}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Integer count of deny/warn/violation rules across all Rego files, e.g. 34

how_to_obtain.instruction: List enabled Sentinel policies in a Terraform Cloud/Enterprise workspace
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TFC_TOKEN' 'https://app.terraform.io/api/v2/organizations/$ORG/policies?filter[enforcement]=hard-mandatory,soft-mandatory' | jq '.meta.pagination.total-count'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response containing total-count of active enforced policies, e.g. 22

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the most recent CI/CD policy validation run logs to confirm rule count reported at scan time
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E '(rules loaded|policies evaluated|checks passed|violations checked)' /var/log/ci/policy-validation.log | tail -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Log lines reporting the number of rules evaluated during the last validation run, e.g. 'Evaluated 89 rules across 12 policy files'

option_description: Controls whether all package and dependency declarations across manifests use exact, immutable version strings instead of floating ranges (^, ~, >=), wildcards (*), or the 'latest' tag, ensuring reproducible builds.
security_impact: The Rego policy `dependency_and_package_version_pinning` requires `input.version_pinning_enforced == true` as a prerequisite alongside lockfile presence and pinning scope. Without version pinning, supply chain substitution attacks become possible — a dependency update between builds could silently introduce a malicious or vulnerable package version.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan package.json for floating version ranges using a Node.js project
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E '"[^"]+":\s*"[\^~><=*]|latest"' package.json && echo 'FLOATING RANGES FOUND' || echo 'No floating ranges detected'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'No floating ranges detected' confirms pinning is enforced; any matched lines indicate violations

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Python requirements.txt for unpinned or range-constrained dependencies
how_to_obtain.command: grep -vE '^(#|$)' requirements.txt | grep -vE '==[0-9]+\.[0-9]+' && echo 'UNPINNED FOUND' || echo 'All pinned'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'All pinned' confirms version pinning; any package lines without == indicate floating declarations

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect go.sum and go.mod to verify all Go module dependencies reference specific hashes and exact versions
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'require' go.mod | grep -vE 'v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+' | grep -v '//'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Empty output confirms all Go dependencies are pinned to exact semantic versions

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review CI/CD pipeline configuration to verify a linting step rejects manifests with floating version ranges before merge
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review the pipeline YAML for steps referencing tools like pip-audit, npm audit, or bundler-audit with --strict flags
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A pipeline stage that explicitly fails on floating versions or enforces lockfile-only installs (e.g., npm ci)

option_description: Controls whether a dependency lockfile appropriate to the project's package manager exists in the repository and is committed to version control, ensuring consistent dependency resolution across all environments.
security_impact: The Rego policy `dependency_and_package_version_pinning` requires `input.lockfile_present == true` in combination with version pinning to activate the supply chain countermeasure. Absent lockfiles allow different dependency versions to be resolved at build time, enabling dependency confusion attacks and build non-reproducibility.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for the presence of common lockfiles in the repository root and confirm they are tracked by git
how_to_obtain.command: for f in package-lock.json yarn.lock Pipfile.lock Gemfile.lock go.sum poetry.lock composer.lock; do git ls-files --error-unmatch $f 2>/dev/null && echo "TRACKED: $f" || echo "MISSING: $f"; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each lockfile relevant to the project stack should show as TRACKED; MISSING indicates it is absent or gitignored

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify lockfiles are not excluded via .gitignore which would prevent them from being committed
how_to_obtain.command: git check-ignore -v package-lock.json yarn.lock Pipfile.lock Gemfile.lock go.sum 2>/dev/null || echo 'No lockfiles gitignored'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'No lockfiles gitignored' confirms lockfiles are not excluded; any matched output indicates a misconfiguration

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect CI/CD pipeline configuration to confirm dependency installation uses lockfile-enforcing commands
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E '(npm ci|pip install -r|bundle install|go mod download|poetry install --no-root)' .github/workflows/*.yml .gitlab-ci.yml 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Commands like 'npm ci' (not 'npm install') confirm lockfile is actively consumed during builds

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the repository in GitHub/GitLab web interface to confirm lockfile presence and last commit date
how_to_obtain.navigation: Navigate to the repository root in GitHub/GitLab > verify lockfile appears in the file listing > click the file to confirm it has recent commit history and is not empty
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lockfile is visible in the repository root with a commit timestamp consistent with recent dependency changes

option_description: Controls the breadth of version pinning across the dependency tree, distinguishing between full pinning of all transitive dependencies, pinning of only direct dependencies, or no pinning at all.
security_impact: The Rego policy activates `dependency_and_package_version_pinning` for both 'full' and 'direct_only' scopes when combined with `version_pinning_enforced == true` and `lockfile_present == true`. However, 'direct_only' leaves transitive dependencies uncontrolled — a vector for dependency confusion and supply chain attacks through indirect packages. 'none' fails both policy conditions entirely.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Determine if pip freeze captures the full transitive dependency tree versus only top-level packages
how_to_obtain.command: pip install pipdeptree 2>/dev/null; pipdeptree --warn silence | grep -c '  -' && echo 'Transitive deps pinned in requirements' || echo 'Only direct deps listed'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A count of transitive dependency lines confirms full tree; if requirements.txt only lists top-level packages it is direct_only

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check if package-lock.json or yarn.lock contains resolved entries for all nested packages (transitive)
how_to_obtain.command: node -e "const l=require('./package-lock.json'); const keys=Object.keys(l.packages||l.dependencies||{}); console.log('Total pinned entries:', keys.length, keys.length > Object.keys(require('./package.json').dependencies||{}).length ? '(includes transitive - FULL)' : '(direct only)')"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If total pinned entries significantly exceeds direct dependency count, scope is 'full'; if roughly equal, scope is 'direct_only'

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use cargo or go tooling to assess whether the lockfile resolves the full dependency graph
how_to_obtain.command: go mod graph | wc -l && cat go.mod | grep -c 'require' && echo 'Compare: graph line count >> require count = full transitive pinning'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: go.sum entries covering all transitive modules indicates 'full' scope; go.sum absent or sparse indicates 'direct_only' or 'none'

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review dependency management documentation or CI pipeline scripts to determine if transitive dependency pinning is a stated requirement
how_to_obtain.navigation: Check internal runbooks, CONTRIBUTING.md, or security policy documentation for statements about transitive dependency pinning requirements
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation explicitly stating all transitive dependencies must be pinned confirms 'full' scope intent

option_description: Controls whether a centralized, dedicated repository of configuration templates for environment provisioning exists and is actively referenced by deployment pipelines, rather than relying on ad-hoc or per-team configuration definitions.
security_impact: The Rego policy `operational_maintainability_of_config_templates` requires `input.template_repository_exists == true` as the foundational condition. Without a central template repository, configurations drift between environments, security baselines cannot be consistently enforced, and there is no authoritative source of truth for what a compliant environment looks like.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search GitHub/GitLab organization for repositories named with common IaC template conventions
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer $GITHUB_TOKEN' 'https://api.github.com/orgs/$ORG/repos?per_page=100' | jq '[.[] | select(.name | test("(infra|config|template|iac|platform|baseline)"; "i"))] | .[].full_name'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of repository names matching IaC/configuration template naming patterns; empty result indicates no dedicated template repository

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to the organization's source control platform and inspect the repository list for a dedicated configuration templates repository
how_to_obtain.navigation: GitHub/GitLab > Organization > Repositories > Search for 'infra', 'templates', 'iac', 'platform-config' > verify repository contains Terraform modules, Helm charts, Ansible roles, or similar IaC artifacts
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A repository exists containing organized configuration templates with subdirectories for environment types (dev, staging, prod)
